entry.title: Magnific One: Every AI image looks the same. Here's how we're fixing it.
entry.summary: Write a few words and get an image that looks art-directed and stays on brand. Here’s what Magnific One does, how people reacted in a blind test, and how to try it unlimited until October 15.
entry.content:
Write a few words and get an image that looks art-directed and stays on brand. Here’s what Magnific One does, how people reacted in a blind test, and how to try it unlimited until October 15.

Every AI image now looks like every other AI image. Same light. Same faces. Same posters.

We built Magnific One to fix that: an image model with art direction built in.

Here’s what it does, how people reacted in a blind test, how we launched it, and how to try it.

Magnific One does three things other image models don’t.

Aesthetics: every image looks directed

You write a few words. Magnific One adds what an art director would: the composition, the light, the camera angle.

That changes how you prompt. Short prompts work better than you’d think: some of our favorite images started with a single word, like “cinematic” or “documentary”. Say what matters, and let the model do the directing.

“Having something that feels like an Art Director guiding the creative process opens up so many possibilities.”
— Azed, creator

Draft mode: explore before you commit

Most of art direction is choosing. Draft gives you 8 or 16 different directions from one prompt, for the price of one image, so you can see your options before you commit. Pick the one you like and make it final, in 2K or 4K.

Brand Kit: your brand in every image

Set up your brand once, from your website, a PDF or a few images. Brand Kit captures your palette, type, imagery and tone, and every final image follows it, whoever on the team is generating.

The more it knows, the more it looks like you. Add a written guideline, up to 50 reference images, and simple rules like “logo bottom left”.

“Within a couple of hours of going back and forth with the agent, we were able to create such a breadth of content that’s all on brand and ready to go.”
— Rourke Heath, CEO and founder, GenHQ

In a blind test, people chose Magnific One

Before launch, we ran a blind test. Voters saw two images made from the same prompt by different models, without knowing which model made which, and picked the one they preferred. Five models took part: Magnific One, Midjourney, GPT Image 2, Nano Banana 2 and Seedream 5 Pro.

We opened it to creators, partners and business customers outside Magnific. Magnific One was the only model to win more than half of its matchups: people preferred its image almost two times out of three.

Or test it yourself. In the Image Generator, select Magnific One and the model you use today, run the same prompt, and compare.

Why we built it

AI images are easy to make. Hard to make right.

Our team has spent years learning what makes an image good. But there was no place to put that knowledge. And our users had thirty models and no way to choose. So we built the image model we wanted ourselves, made for the work marketing and brand teams do every day.

Launch night in Singapore

On October 8, I showed Magnific One for the first time, at our Upscale Day in Singapore. We had chosen an art gallery for it: the perfect setting to launch an image model with art direction built in. Every piece on the wall had been chosen, placed and lit by someone with taste. That’s art direction. That’s what Magnific One is about.

I’m usually a bit nervous before I go on stage. This time, I wasn’t. I was just excited. Excited to finally show the world what we’d built.

I finished my last slide. And then, applause.

Months of work, on the technology behind Magnific One and on the launch itself, came down to that moment. At 21:30 in Singapore, 15:30 in Madrid, Magnific One went live everywhere.

The first day

In the first 24 hours, thousands of people made images with Magnific One, and many of them set up their own Brand Kit.

We even made real cereal boxes for the night: Magnific One, "Art direction, built in", fortified with Brand Kit. People took them home.

“With my own characters and styles, it's really damn good!”
— Paige Piskin, creator

Plans and pricing

Magnific One is available on all paid plans, in 2K or 4K and in High or Max quality. You’ll find the current credits for each option on our Pricing page.

Try it, unlimited

Until October 15, Magnific One is unlimited in the Magnific desktop app for Premium+, Pro and Business.

We're creatives too. This one means a lot to us. Come see what it can do.

Try Magnific One

entry.title: AI videos can be 30 seconds long. People ask for 5
entry.summary: Across 107 million AI videos generated on Magnific and Freepik between November 2025 and August 2026, the median clip people asked for was 5 seconds long and 71% of clips were exactly 5 or 10 seconds.
entry.content:
Across 107 million AI videos generated on Magnific and Freepik between November 2025 and August 2026, the median clip people asked for was 5 seconds long and 71% of clips were exactly 5 or 10 seconds.

Creative Signals · VideoData: Nov 2025 – Aug 2026Published Sep 2026

Across 107 million AI videos generated on the platform between November 2025 and August 2026, the clip people asked for was 5 seconds long more often than anything else, and 7 in 10 requests were exactly 5 or 10 seconds.

In those 10 months the models learned to go longer. The requests didn’t follow: where a model allows more than 10 seconds, 1 clip in 7 takes it, and that share fell rather than rose.

  • Median length

    5s

    Mean 7.1s. The video delivered matches the request within half a second 99.3% of the time

    is the median length people ask an AI video model for

  • Two presets

    71%

    99.8% are 15s or shorter; 0.06% are 30s

    of AI videos are exactly 5s or 10s long

  • Longer options

    1 in 7

    Those models went from 19% to 60% of all videos; the share of clips taking the extra seconds fell, from 20% to 15%

    clips on models that allow more than 10s go past 10s

  • Total footage

    24 years

    754.5 million seconds, 209,584 hours; clips of 10s or more are 35% of the videos and 52% of the time

    of AI video generated in 10 months

Section 01

Most AI videos are 5 seconds long

The length of an AI video is set by two presets. 41.2% of the videos generated on the platform were 5 seconds long and 30.1% were 10 seconds; the next most common lengths, 6 and 4 seconds, add 7.9% and 7.0%.

The median request is 5 seconds and the mean 7.1. 99.8% of videos are 15 seconds or shorter; 1 in 20 goes over 10 seconds; fewer than 1 in 500 goes over 15; 30-second clips are 0.06% of the total, and nothing longer exists at any scale: the handful of records above 30 seconds are logging noise, not clips people made. The people searching for how to make a 1-minute AI video are looking for something that, in 107 million generations, almost nobody made in one pass. Length does add up, though: those clips are 754.5 million seconds of video, 209,584 hours, 24 years of footage in 10 months, and the 10-second-and-up clips carry more than half of it (52%) while being a third of the count.

The video lasts what you asked for

“Requested length” could be a setting nobody gets. It isn’t. Matching each generation to the length of the file it produced, 99.3% of videos land within half a second of the request. The median delivered video runs 5.04 seconds: 5 seconds and a single frame at 24 frames per second. 0.6% run more than a second longer than requested. So when this report says people ask for 5 seconds, that is also what they get. Extending a clip after generating it is a separate flow, and it was 0.04% of the volume in 10 months.

Section 02

Longer clips doubled, and it's the models, not the people

Videos longer than 10 seconds went from 4.0% of the total in November 2025 to 8.9% in August 2026. Clips of 15 seconds or more went from 0.02% to 5.3%; 30-second clips appeared in August and were 0.7% of that month.

The average clip barely moved, from 6.8 to 7.1 seconds, because the other end grew too: 5 seconds or less went from 46% to 56% of videos, and the 10-second preset lost nearly 8 points, from 29% to 21%. The middle emptied into both ends. What did not change is how often people take the extra seconds when a model offers them. In November, 19% of videos were made on a model that allows more than 10 seconds; in August, 60%, three times as many. Inside those models, the share of clips that actually go over 10 seconds peaked at 20% in November, the first month, sat between 12% and 17% every month after that, and was 15% in August; over the whole window, 1 in 7. A decomposition by model says the same thing: the rise in long clips comes from which models people use, and almost none of it from people asking the same model for more.

The 10-second preset is what's shrinking

Both ends grew at the expense of the middle. Inside the models that offer only 5 or 10 seconds, the 10-second option lost ground: on Kling 2.5, the most used video model, 10-second clips fell from 46.5% of its generations in November to 41.3% in August; on Hailuo 2.3, from 48.7% to 35.3%. Meanwhile the new models with 15- and 30-second caps brought the long tail. The result is a distribution with more 5-second clips and more 15-second clips than in November, and fewer 10-second ones.

Section 03

The higher the limit, the fewer people reach it

Give people two lengths and they split down the middle. On Kling 2.5, which offers 5 or 10 seconds, 48.8% of clips are 10 seconds; on Hailuo 2.3, with 6 or 10, 50.8% take the 10; on Veo 3.1, capped at 8 seconds on the platform, 41.7% take the 8.

Raise the limit to 15 seconds and the top stops being popular: between 4.7% and 9.6% of clips on Kling 3.0, Kling o3, HappyHorse 1.1 and Seedance 2.0 are 15 seconds, and the median on every one of them is back at 5 seconds. Taken together, the models that allow 15 seconds made 28 million videos: 57% of them 5 seconds or shorter, 12.6% longer than 10, 7.4% at the 15-second cap. Seedance 2.5, the first model on the platform to allow 30 seconds, has a median clip of 7 seconds; 8.8% of its generations ask for the full 30, and 36.6% ask for 5 or less. Wan 3.0, also capped at 30, is at 6.3%. The exception is Sora 2, with a median of 8 seconds and 47.9% of clips over 10. Its shortest option is 4 seconds and the next is 8; it has no 5-second preset to fall back on. The default, not the ceiling, is what decides how long an AI video is.

It isn't the interface

If 5 seconds were just the web app’s default, developers would ask for something else. They don’t. Since June 9, 2026, when API, MCP and agent traffic can be attributed, videos requested without an interface have the same median (5 seconds) and the same mean (7.0 seconds) as videos requested in the web app, and 5 seconds or less is even more common: 58% against 56%. Developers do reach past 10 seconds a little more often, 11.1% against 7.5% in the web app, and 15 seconds or more almost twice as often, 7.8% against 4.1%. Traffic without an interface is 2.8% of videos in that period. The 5-second clip is what people ask for when nothing suggests it.

Window

November 1, 2025 to August 31, 2026 (UTC), 10 complete calendar months. Monthly volume is not published as a trend: generations follow platform traffic, and this report measures proportions. The surface comparison uses only the period from June 9, 2026, when API, MCP and agent traffic can be attributed.

Population

Successful video generations on the platform’s video generator flows (Freepik and Magnific combined), all surfaces except internal traffic, generation models only: 108,302,430 generations, the same population as One AI video model made 4 in 10 videos. Four services that share the flow name but output no video (a moderation pass, a music model, two internal utilities) are excluded, as in that report. Length is the requested length of each generation, in seconds, as configured when the clip was made. Generations with no positive length are removed: 1,604,976 rows, 1.5%, leaving 106,697,454 videos for every percentage in this report.

Definitions

“5 seconds” includes the 5.1-second setting of one integration route; “over 10 seconds” means strictly more than 10. A model allows more than 10 seconds when at least 0.5% of its generations in the window are longer than 10 seconds; 28 models qualify. A model’s cap is the longest length that at least 0.5% of its generations request; it is the cap as seen on the platform, which can differ from the maximum the vendor advertises or from extension features.

Delivered length comes from the credits ledger, which records the measured length of the file produced and falls back to the requested value when no file measurement exists; the comparison uses the exact one-to-one match between generation and transaction, available from January 26, 2026, and covers 84.6 million videos, 79% of the population. Models are named by provider, model and version; the same model served through two integration routes appears as two rows in the data and is named once in the text. Full definitions in the Report Glossary.

Limitations

1. Length is what people asked for, not what they were willing to pay for
Longer clips cost more credits, and this report cannot separate a preference for short clips from a preference for cheaper ones.
2. 1.5% of generations have no recorded length, and they are not random
94% of them are two models, Kling 2.6 (24.8% of its rows) and Kling 3.0 (3.9%), and where the credits ledger measured those files, their median is 9.9 seconds. If all of them were counted, the share of videos over 10 seconds would rise by at most 0.6 points over the window and 0.3 points in August.
3. One integration route records half the length it delivers
On one route for Wan 2.2 (0.7% of videos) the recorded length is half the delivered one; those rows are kept as recorded and sit in the 4-seconds-or-less and 5-second buckets.
4. Delivered length is measured for most models, not all
It falls back to the requested value on some models, Veo 3.1 above all; that is why the report gives one platform-wide reliability figure and no per-model comparison.
5. A few hundred records are logging noise
319 generations, 0.0003%, record lengths above 30 seconds, up to 1,555 seconds, on models that offer no such option; they are kept in the totals and shown as 0.0%.
6. Caps are what the platform offers, not what a model can do elsewhere
Sora 2's 20 seconds, Veo 3.1's 8 and Kling 3.0's 15 are the options available here; extension features are a separate flow with 42,295 generations in the window, 0.04% of the volume, and are not part of these figures.
7. The monthly median is a preset, not a trend
The median request is 5 seconds every month, or 6 in months when the 6-second presets weigh more; monthly change is read from the mean and from the shares of each length, not from the median.

Reproducibility

Every number was independently recomputed by a second pass with its own queries before publication: the population and the clean rows, the length distribution and its buckets, total seconds, the ten monthly rows, the availability and uptake series under its strict definition, the per-model figures for Kling 2.5, Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.5 and Sora 2, the surface comparison, the delivered-length match, and the check that every model in the population outputs video. Nineteen counter-queries and three follow-ups, all reproduced.

Cite & data

Cite this report

Citation

Magnific (2026). AI videos can be 30 seconds long. People ask for 5. Creative Signals, September 2026. magnific.com/blog/ai-video-length

Short form for press

“Across 107 million AI videos generated on Magnific and Freepik between November 2025 and August 2026, the median clip people asked for was 5 seconds long and 71% of clips were exactly 5 or 10 seconds. Models that allow more than 10 seconds went from 19% to 60% of all videos in that time, but only 1 clip in 7 made on them goes over 10 seconds, a share that fell over the period. In total, 24 years of AI video were generated in 10 months.”

entry.title: It takes about 4 AI images to keep one
entry.summary: Across 906 million successful AI image generations on Magnific and Freepik between February and August 2026, people downloaded 1 image for every 4 they generated in the image generator, and 1 for every 4.6 across all image tools.
entry.content:
Across 906 million successful AI image generations on Magnific and Freepik between February and August 2026, people downloaded 1 image for every 4 they generated in the image generator, and 1 for every 4.6 across all image tools.

Creative Signals · ImageData: Feb–Aug 2026Published Sep 2026

Pricing pages tell you what one image costs. They don’t count how many you make before you keep one. Across 906 million successful image generations on Freepik and Magnific between February and August 2026, people using the web app downloaded 1 image for every 4 they generated in the image generator, 1 for every 4.6 across all image tools.

A generation costs 75 credits at list price half the time; the image you keep, about 300. Each try got 46% more expensive over the 7 months. People needed 23% fewer of them.

  • Generations per kept image

    4 generations

    4.6 across all image tools. The typical user: 6

    for every image downloaded from the image generator

  • Cost of one generation

    75 credits

    4 in 5 generations cost 50 or 75 credits at list price

    is the median cost of one generation

  • Cost of a kept image

    About 300 credits

    284 in the image generator, 321 across all image tools; a median session costs 250

    per image you keep

  • Tries per kept image

    −23%

    4.7 to 3.6 in the image generator, where a generation went from 59 to 84 list-price credits

    generations per kept image, Feb to Aug 2026

Section 01

1 download for every 4 generations

One image is almost never the end of it. A working session, consecutive generations by the same person in the same tool with less than 10 minutes between them, has a median of 4 generations. 18.6% of sessions stop after 1; 57% stop at 4 or fewer; 1 in 10 runs past 20, and those sessions produce half of all the generations this report counts.

Downloads tell the same story from the other end. In the image generator, people downloaded 1 image for every 4.0 they generated. In Talk to image, 1 for every 4.8; in Spaces, where a workflow generates several images per step, 1 for every 5.7. Across every image tool, 1 for every 4.6. Weight each user the same instead of each image and the typical user sits at 6 generations per download, because the heaviest users generate the most and keep the smallest share. 3 in 4 days a person uses the image generator end with at least one download; 1 in 4 end with nothing kept.

A session is not 4 attempts

The interface generates in batches of 4, and it shows: sessions of exactly 4 are 1.8 times as common as sessions of 3 and 3.3 times as common as sessions of 5. Each image in a batch is its own request and its own charge, so a batch of 4 costs 4 generations, but one click can produce a 4-generation session. That is why this report counts generations per session and downloads per generation, not “attempts.” The median holds: 4 with a 10-minute gap, 5 with a 30-minute gap, 4 when the tool is ignored. The mean does not: 8 generations per session at 10 minutes in August, 12 at 30. Every average in this report says which definition it uses.

Section 02

The image you keep costs about 300 credits

One generation costs 75 credits in 48% of cases and 50 credits in another 33%. The median is 75; the mean over priced generations, 72. 6% of generations cost 25 credits or less, 9% cost 100 or more.

The list price is the model: Seedream 4.5, Nano Banana, and Seedream 4 at 50 credits; Nano Banana 2, Nano Banana Pro, and Seedream 5 at 75; GPT Image 2 from 15 to 260 depending on quality, 45 at the median and 173 on average. Count every generation, the free ones included, and divide by the downloads: the kept image comes out at 284 credits in the image generator, 331 in Talk to image, 445 in Spaces, 321 across all image tools. The median session costs 250 credits, 3 to 4 generations at 75; 300 if only sessions with a priced generation count. 2 in 3 generations run on unlimited plans, where the credit is a list price, not a charge; on the plans that pay per generation, the mean was 69 credits in February and 99 in August.

Unlimited plans generate more per session

The plan moves the session more than the price does. In the 31–99 credit range, where 3 in 4 sessions happen, a session on an unlimited plan averages 11.8 generations; one that pays per generation, 8.1. Unlimited sessions average more generations in every price range, though the median is 4 in both. Price shows up at the top: among sessions that pay per generation, 1 in 3 stops after a single image when the model costs 100 credits or more, against 1 in 5 in the 31–99 range. Agents stop soonest of all. Since June, 43% of sessions run through AI agents are a single generation, against 19% in the web app. Agents generate and leave. People iterate.

Section 03

Each try costs 46% more—the kept image, 9 to 19%

In February 2026 the average generation cost 60 credits at list price. In August, 88, up 46%. Almost none of that is price changes.

At each model’s window price the average would have risen just as much, because people moved to pricier models: Seedream 4.5, at 50 credits, went from 37% of priced generations to 4.5%; Seedream 5 Pro 2K, at 75 credits, went from 0 to 26%; Nano Banana 2 Flash 1K and 2K, both at 75 credits by August, from 1.4% to 26%. Within a model the prices moved little, and in both directions: the one clear cut went against the trend, Nano Banana 2 Flash 2K from 100 credits down to 75. Over the same 7 months people needed fewer generations per kept image. In the image generator the ratio fell every month, from 4.7 in February to 3.6 in August, down 23%. Sessions over 20 generations went from 12% to 8%, while the median session stayed at 4. The credits per kept image absorbed most of it: 278 in February, 302 in August, up 9% in the image generator and 19% across the tools that kept the same name all year. The try got much more expensive. The image you keep, much less.

New users make more tries, and many are free

A person in their first week on the platform generates 5.5 images per download; a person with 3 to 12 months, 4.5. In the image generator the gap is wider, 5.3 against 3.9. Only 44% of a new user’s days in the tool end with a download, against 64% for a user of 3 to 12 months. Their credits per kept image are about the same, 314 against 321, for one reason: 18% of a first-week user’s generations are free, 28% in August, and free generations count as tries, not as cost. New users don’t pay the same. They try more, and a good part of the trying is free.

Window

February 1 to August 31, 2026 (UTC), 7 complete calendar months. The window starts in February because the identifier that links a generation to its credit charge and its user exists from January 19, 2026. Monthly volume is not published as a trend: generations follow platform traffic, and this report measures ratios. The surface comparison uses the period from June 9, 2026, when API, MCP, and agent traffic can be attributed.

Population

Successful image generations on the platform’s image generation flows (Freepik and Magnific combined), all surfaces except internal traffic: 906,480,782 generations, the population of the two previous image reports restricted to the window. 852,592,410 of them, 94.1%, link to a credit record that carries the user, the tool, and the list-price credits; coverage rises from 92.8% in February to 99.35% in August. The generations that don’t link sit on the cheapest routes, so the cost figures are, if anything, understated in February and the 46% rise is a floor. Percentages about cost use the 829,144,478 linked generations with a list price; sessions use the linked generations; the download ratio uses the 821,287,756 linked generations made in the web app, 576,130,208 of them in the image generator.

Definitions

Credits are list-price credits: what a generation costs on a plan that pays per image. Generations on unlimited plans, 65% of priced generations, count at that list price even though the plan does not charge them one by one; their share fell from 78% in February to 46% in August. Free generations, 2.5% of the linked total and only from April, count as generations and as zero credits. Refunded generations, 0.3%, are left out of cost. Charges are per request; 98.5% of requests return one image, so credits per generation and credits per request are the same figure. A session is a run of generations by the same user in the same tool with less than 10 minutes between consecutive generations, dated by its first one.

A download is a download or copy event recorded for the same user, in the same tool, on the same day (UTC) as the generations; copies are 1.5% of the total. No record links a download to the image it belongs to, so this report never says which image was kept, only how many were generated for each one downloaded; both sides are restricted to the web app. Downloads on days without a generation in the same tool are not counted; 2 in 3 of them belong to tools outside this population. Adding every one of them would take the all-tools ratio from 4.6 to 3.8; the defensible range is 3.9 to 4.6. The per-user figure, 6 generations per download for the typical user, is the median over 1,085,259 users with at least 5 generations and 1 download, counted with downloads from every surface. Tools follow the credit record: the image generator, Spaces, Talk to image, and the editing tools. In July the platform renamed its retouch flow into Talk to image on both the generation and the download side, which breaks the all-tools download series; the monthly series is therefore shown for the image generator, whose share of days with a download is flat across the window. Tenure is the time since the user’s registration date on the day of the generation; 0.1% of user-days and 0.05% of sessions carry a registration date later than the generation and are excluded. Models carry their public names; the same model served through several routes is one row. Full definitions in the Report Glossary.

Limitations

1. The download ratio is an aggregate, not a per-image attribution
It counts downloads and generations by the same user in the same tool on the same day. It cannot say which generation was kept, and it counts an image downloaded twice as two downloads.
2. A session is a definition, not an observation of intent
Its median survives the 10-minute gap and the tool boundary; its mean does not, and rises from 8 to 12 generations in August with a 30-minute gap. Where a mean appears, its definition is next to it.
3. The interface generates in batches of 4
Each image in a batch is a separate request. A 4-generation session can be a single click.
4. Credits are list prices
On unlimited plans, 65% of priced generations, the marginal cost of a generation is zero, and those sessions average more generations at every price. The credits per kept image are what the same images would cost on a pay-per-image plan.
5. The rise in credits per generation is a change in which models people use, not in what models cost
At fixed prices the average rises as much as it did. Weighted by February's mix, prices within a model add 4 credits; weighted by August's, they subtract 5, because one model's price fell from 100 to 75. Both are small next to the 28-credit rise.
6. The editing tools are left out of the download ratio
They are 9.5% of generations, and their results are applied on the canvas and rarely produce a download event.
7. Sample-free, but not drift-free
The population moves by about 0.002% between runs as the data warehouse refreshes, which explains differences of a few hundred rows between tables.

Reproducibility

A second pass with its own queries recomputed the population and coverage, the credit distribution, the monthly means, the session statistics, the download ratios on a consistent base, the tenure buckets, and the price-by-plan table before publication, in two rounds: the first found 4 blocking issues and 11 corrections, among them the download base and the July renaming; the second verified the corrected figures and added 4 precision corrections.

Cite & data

Cite this report

Citation

Magnific (2026). It takes about 4 AI images to keep one. Creative Signals, September 2026. magnific.com/blog/cost-of-a-kept-image

Short form for press

“Across 906 million successful AI image generations on Magnific and Freepik between February and August 2026, people using the web app downloaded 1 image for every 4 they generated in the image generator, and 1 for every 4.6 across all image tools. A generation cost 75 credits at list price half the time, and the image kept about 300. Between February and August the average generation went from 60 to 88 credits, up 46%, as people moved to pricier models, while the generations per kept image fell from 4.7 to 3.6. The kept image went from 278 to 302 credits, up 9%, and up 19% across the tools that kept the same name all year.”

entry.title: 1 in 3 AI image prompts now tops 150 words

entry.content:
Across 1.22 billion prompts sent to AI image models on Magnific and Freepik between November 2025 and August 2026, the median prompt was 49 words and 3 in 10 prompts were 20 words or fewer. Prompts over 150 words went from 8% of the total in November to 31% in August.

Creative Signals · ImageData: Nov 2025 – Aug 2026Published Sep 2026

The guides say to describe the subject, the style, the light, and the lens. Across 1.22 billion prompts sent to AI image models between November 2025 and August 2026, half were under 50 words and 3 in 10 were 20 words or fewer.

The other end is where the change is: prompts over 150 words went from 1 in 12 in November to 1 in 3 in August, and the short ones barely moved.

  • Median prompt

    49 words

    1 in 4 is 17 words or fewer; 1 in 4 is over 125

    is the median AI image prompt

  • Long prompts

    1 in 3

    1 in 12 in Nov 2025. Prompts of 20 words or fewer: 29% in both months

    prompts in Aug 2026 ran over 150 words

  • With an image

    76%

    1 in 3 of those is 20 words or fewer; 1 in 8 starts with an edit verb

    of prompts come with an image attached

  • English vs local

    2–8×

    Brazil 137 vs 36 words, Korea 126 vs 15, Spain 101 vs 29. English is 2 in 3 prompts, down from 3 in 4

    longer: the English prompt vs the local-language prompt, in the same country

Section 01

Half of all AI image prompts are under 50 words

The median prompt sent to an AI image model is 49 words. A quarter of prompts are 17 words or fewer; a quarter run past 125. 30% are 20 words or fewer, 49% sit between 21 and 150, and 21% are longer than 150.

That last fifth is where the text is: prompts over 150 words carry 65% of all the words the models received in 10 months, and the short ones, 3 in 10 prompts, carry 3%. 4 in 10 prompts ask for quality with the words the guides recommend, like realistic, cinematic, or 4K, and that share has barely moved in 10 months, 40% to 38%. Two kinds of prompt live in these numbers, and they don’t look alike: the one-line instruction and the brief.

3 in 4 prompts come with an image

76% of prompts arrive with an image attached, as a reference or as the thing to change. 34% are 20 words or fewer, against 17% of prompts sent with text alone. 12% open with an edit verb like make, change, remove, or add; with text alone, fewer than 1% do. 34% point at a numbered image; with text alone, under 1%. The median is 42 words with an image and 62 without. Text-only prompts are the ones that describe: 53% carry a quality word and 26% a style word, against 35% and 11% of prompts with an image. The prompt people write most often does not describe a picture from scratch. It comes with one.

Section 02

Long prompts went from 1 in 12 to 1 in 3, and the short ones stayed

In November 2025, 8.4% of prompts ran over 150 words. In August 2026, 31.5% did. Prompts over 300 words went from 0.8% to 16.7%. The median moved from 42 to 60 words.

What did not move is the short end: prompts of 20 words or fewer were 29.2% of the total in November and 28.8% in August, and between 28.3% and 32.2% every month in between. What emptied is the middle: prompts between 21 and 150 words fell from 62% to 40%, 23 points that went whole to the long end. The long end also changed shape. 1.2% of prompts carried markdown formatting in November, bold marks, headings, bullet lists; 11.6% did in August, 1 in 9. Prompts that say what to avoid went from 20% to 39%. The quality words went from 40% to 38%. People did not stop typing one line. They added a second way of prompting: the structured brief, often carrying the formatting of another tool.

It isn't the models, the agents, or the images

We checked three other explanations. It isn’t the models: on Nano Banana Pro, available the whole window, prompts over 150 words went from 12.7% in November to 44.4% in August; on Nano Banana, from 3.0% to 29.1%; on Seedream 4, from 10.8% to 35.7%. Prompts sent to Nano Banana 2 and Nano Banana Pro have a median of 70 to 74 words; to Seedream 4.5, 35. It isn’t the agents: prompts sent through APIs, MCP clients, and agents were 0.5% of the total in November and 4.0% in August, and inside the web app alone the long share went from 8.4% to 31.2%. It isn’t the images: prompts with an image attached went from 7.3% long to 30.9%, and prompts without one from 9.3% to 33.9%. On the same models, in the same app, people write longer prompts than they did 10 months ago.

Section 03

English is the language of the long prompt

2 in 3 prompts are written in English: 67% over the window, and falling, from 76% in November to 62% in August, as Portuguese, Spanish, and Russian grew. Length follows language. The median English prompt is 67 words; in Spanish it is 27, in Portuguese 33, in Russian 23, in Korean 15.

1 in 4 English prompts runs over 150 words; in every other language written with spaces, between 1 in 5 and 1 in 17. Among prompts from users in Brazil, 44% are in English and 45% in Portuguese; the English ones have a median of 137 words, the Portuguese ones 36. In Korea, 44% are in English, with a median of 126 words against 15 in Korean. In Spain, 49% in English: 101 words against 29. The same user base writes two ways: a long English brief, and a short instruction in their own language.

Agents don't write short prompts

Since June 2026, when API, MCP, and agent traffic can be told apart, prompts sent without an interface have a median of 116 words, against 54 in the web app, and only 3% of them are 20 words or fewer, against 31%. When Claude writes the prompt, the median is 128 words and 1% of its prompts are 20 words or fewer; when ChatGPT does, the median is 186 and 2% are. The exceptions are the Photoshop and Figma plugins, with medians of 18 and 23 words: a person typing an edit into their own tool. Agents also don’t repeat themselves. In two weeks of August, 53% of generations in the web app were run again with the identical prompt within 10 minutes; through APIs and agents, 9%. 7 in 10 generations were followed by a different prompt from the same user within 10 minutes: 63% for prompts of 5 words or fewer, 70% to 75% for prompts over 20 words. A longer prompt does not get run again less often. It is more often followed by a new one.

Window

November 1, 2025 to August 31, 2026 (UTC), 10 complete calendar months. Monthly volume is not published as a trend: generations follow platform traffic, and this report measures proportions. The surface comparison uses the period from June 9, 2026, when API, MCP, and agent traffic can be attributed, and the client breakdown the period from June 24, 2026. The re-run analysis covers August 10 to 23, 2026.

Population

Successful image generations on the platform’s image generation flows (Freepik and Magnific combined), all surfaces except internal traffic: 1,230,214,786 generations, the population of No AI image model stayed on top for six months, refreshed. The prompt is the text the model received: every positive text element of the request, in order; negative prompts (1.0% of generations) are not part of it. 1,219,991,231 generations carry a prompt, 99.2%, and every percentage in this report uses them as its base. Words are whitespace-separated tokens. Scripts written without spaces, Chinese, Japanese, and Thai, 3% of prompts, count as few words and land in the short bucket whatever their real length; limitation 5 sizes that effect, and medians for those languages are not compared.

Definitions

Short = 20 words or fewer; long = over 150 words; the 9 length buckets are fixed. With an image = the request carried at least one image, as a reference or as the image to edit; that split excludes one integration route that does not record image inputs, 4.4% of prompts, and matches the 76% published in the image model report. Markdown formatting = bold marks, headings, bullet or numbered lists at the start of a line; it is a footprint of text written or expanded in another tool, not proof of it. Quality words, style words, says what to avoid, and edit verb are fixed English word lists, so their shares are lower bounds.

Language is identified with fastText on a stratified sample of 60,000 prompts per month, 600,000 in total, with a 0.50 confidence threshold; 3.6% of the sample is undetermined; shares are given over all prompts, so English is 67% of all prompts and 70% of identified ones. Country is the billing country of the user who made the request, available from January 19, 2026, and covers 71% of the sample. Re-run = the same user sends the identical prompt, after normalizing spaces and case, within 10 minutes; requests that produce several images count once. Models are named with their public names; the same model served through two integration routes is one row. Full definitions in the Report Glossary.

Limitations

1. A character limit until February 1, 2026
Until February 1, 2026, no text element longer than about 3,360 characters was stored; the limit was lifted on February 2 on every surface at once. Prompts over 150 words, about 1,000 characters, sit well below it, and the median even more so, so both are compared across the window. The mean, the share over 1,000 words, and the longest prompt are not, because their November value is a ceiling, not a behavior. Removing every August prompt above 4,000 characters, the share over 150 words is 24.9%, still 3 times November, and the share over 300 words is 10.2%, still 13 times.
2. Appended style text
Some product flows append style text to what the user typed. Where the placeholder was left unfilled it is visible, in 1.5% of prompts; where it was filled it is not. Excluding the flows involved would move the short share by at most 1.2 points.
3. Fixed internal prompts
Two integration routes send a fixed internal prompt of 6 to 8 words, 0.4% of prompts. They are kept in the totals and left out of the per-model figures.
4. English word lists
The English word lists behind quality, style, avoidance, and edit-verb shares miss the same idea in Spanish or Portuguese. English fell from 76% to 62% of prompts in the window, so the November-to-August change in those shares is, if anything, understated.
5. Roughly flat, not exactly flat
The short share is roughly flat, not exactly flat: among prompts in Latin script it went from 27.4% to 25.4%, and the growth of scripts without spaces, from 3.2% to 7.0% of prompts, holds the total steady.
6. Long prompts are not re-run less often
The apparent decline by length in the pooled figure comes from the mix of web and API traffic. Within the web app the re-run rate is between 49.7% and 55.2% at every length.
7. A sample, not the full population
Language and country come from a sample, not from the full population; a difference of 1 point between months is inside its noise.

Reproducibility

A second pass with its own queries recomputed the population and prompt coverage, the 9 length buckets, the quantiles and total words, the November and August rows, the two-segment decomposition, the within-model series for 4 models, the surface and client figures, the marker counts, the fixed-prompt routes, and the re-run rates by length and surface before publication: 24 counter-queries and 9 corrections, among them the character limit of the first three months and the exclusion of the route that does not record images. Language, country, and follow-up figures were checked for internal consistency, not recomputed.

Cite & data

Cite this report

Citation

Magnific (2026). 1 in 3 AI image prompts now tops 150 words. Creative Signals, September 2026. magnific.com/blog/how-people-prompt

Short form for press

“Across 1.22 billion prompts sent to AI image models on Magnific and Freepik between November 2025 and August 2026, the median prompt was 49 words and 3 in 10 prompts were 20 words or fewer. Prompts over 150 words went from 8% of the total in November to 31% in August while the share of short prompts stayed at roughly 29%. 76% of prompts came with an image attached. English was 2 in 3 prompts and, in each of the 8 countries compared, the English prompt was 2 to 8 times longer than the one in the local language.”

entry.title: No AI image model stayed on top for six months
entry.summary: The most used AI image model changed three times in ten months, across 1.2 billion images generated on Magnific and Freepik between November 2025 and August 2026.
entry.content:
The most used AI image model changed three times in ten months, across 1.2 billion images generated on Magnific and Freepik between November 2025 and August 2026.

Creative Signals · ImageData: Nov 2025 – Aug 2026Published Sep 2026

Across 1.2 billion image generations on the platform between November 2025 and August 2026, the most used model changed hands three times.

In AI video, the leader never moved. In AI image, nobody kept the top spot for more than 5 months, and the model that won the window took just one in five images.

  • Most used models

    4

    Seedream 4, Seedream 4.5, Nano Banana 2, Seedream 5. The top video model never changed.

    different models were the most used in 10 months

  • Window leader

    21.0%

    Kling 2.5 made 39.9% of AI videos in the same period

    of all AI images came from the window leader, Nano Banana 2

  • From peak to half

    3–5 weeks

    The three models that reached first place peaked 8 to 13 weeks after launch; in video, 16

    for a leading image model to lose half its peak share

  • Edits

    3 in 4

    76.0% image-to-image; the three biggest models are 85–87% edits

    AI images start from another image

Section 01

Four different models were the most used in 10 months

Seedream 4 made 43.5% of AI images in November 2025. By January the most used model was Seedream 4.5, by March it was Nano Banana 2, and in August Seedream 5 edged past it, 33.1% to 32.7%.

Over the whole window Nano Banana 2 (Google’s Gemini 3.1 Flash Image) comes first with 21.0%, ByteDance’s Seedream 4.5 second with 19.6%, Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro Image) third with 17.5%. The catalog went from 16 models in use to 30, and the top 5 still made between 77.2% and 91.6% of images every month. This is the same platform where one video model, Kling 2.5, stayed first for all 10 months with 39.9% of videos: image is a different market. Models don’t die, they get replaced by their own successors: Seedream 4 handed over to Seedream 4.5 and then Seedream 5; Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image) to Nano Banana Pro and then Nano Banana 2.

Two companies made 8 in 10 AI images

Look at makers instead of models and the churn disappears. Google made 47.4% of the images in the window and ByteDance 33.8%, 81.2% between them; with Black Forest Labs, three companies made 93.2%. Google moved between 35% and 57% of a month and ByteDance between 26% and 45%, while their models replaced each other underneath. OpenAI arrived with GPT Image 2 in April and settled at about 7%. Midjourney isn’t on the platform, so it isn’t measured.

Section 02

Winning image models peak in ten weeks and halve in a month

The three models that reached first place took 8, 10 and 13 weeks from launch to their peak share: Nano Banana 2 peaked at 38.2% of a week's images 8 weeks after it crossed 0.5%, Seedream 4.5 at 37.0% after 10, Nano Banana Pro at 33.8% after 13. In video, the biggest launch of the same period took 16.

What follows the peak is faster still. Six models have held more than 30% of a week’s images. Of the four that have since come down, all four lost half of their peak within 3 to 5 weeks: Seedream 4.5 and Nano Banana Pro in 3, Seedream 4 in 4, Nano Banana in 5. Smaller models decline more slowly: Flux 1 Dev took 7 weeks, Flux 2 Klein 10, Flux 2 Pro 20. Three models had not lost half of their peak when the data ends: Nano Banana 2, Seedream 5, GPT Image 2, the three most recent launches to pass 5% of a week’s images. Seedream 5 was still climbing in the last week, at 33.8%, 26 weeks after launch; GPT Image 2 peaked at 8.1% after 11.

Losing half your peak is not dying

Nano Banana Pro lost half of its 33.8% peak in 3 weeks and then stopped falling: it held between 14% and 18% of each month’s images for the next six months, second or third every month from March to August. The time it takes to lose half a peak measures how fast a model comes down from its high, not whether it disappears. Seedream 4.5 lost half its peak in March, the month Nano Banana 2 arrived; by August, Seedream 5 had taken its place inside the same family and ByteDance was back at 37.9% of images, close to its February level. And Nano Banana’s peak sits in the first week of our data, so its 5 weeks are counted from the edge of the window, not from its real peak.

Section 03

The winners are editing models

76.0% of the AI images generated on the platform started from another image: a reference, a photo to edit, a previous generation. Only 24.0% came from text alone.

The three biggest models are the most edit-heavy: 85.2% of Nano Banana 2’s generations, 85.3% of Seedream 4.5’s and 87.0% of Nano Banana Pro’s had an image in the input, and between them they made 67% of all image-to-image generations. Text-to-image lives elsewhere. Flux 2 Klein is 70.3% text-only and Flux 1 Dev 96.5%, and together they made 23% of the text-only images; Imagen 3 and Ideogram 3 are 100.0% text-only. GPT Image 2 is the most balanced of the big ones, at 69.8% edits. The share of edits rose from 63.6% of images in November to 82.0% in August, and almost none of that is people editing more with the same model: inside each model the edit share barely moved, or fell. What changed is which models people use. The ones that won are the ones that edit.

Without an interface, the leader changes

The obvious objection is that all of this is the web app’s defaults. Partly. Since June 9, 2026, when we can attribute API, MCP and agent traffic, the most used model outside the interface is Nano Banana Pro with 33.3%, against 14.3% in the web app; Nano Banana 2, first in the web app with 35.7%, drops to 17.4%. GPT Image 2 nearly doubles its weight, 12.8% against 7.0%. Google as a maker is the same on both sides, 52.1% and 51.2%. The interface picks the fast model; developers pick the Pro one. Traffic without an interface is 2.9% of images in that period; small, but it shows that the concentration in two companies is not a default of the web app.

Window

November 1, 2025 to August 31, 2026 (UTC), 10 complete calendar months, for monthly shares and window totals. Weekly figures (time to peak, half-life) use the 43 complete Monday-to-Sunday weeks inside that window, November 3, 2025 to August 30, 2026. Monthly volume is not published as a trend: generations follow platform traffic, and this report measures proportions.

Population

Successful image generations on the platform’s image generation flows (Freepik and Magnific combined), all surfaces except internal traffic: 1,230,191,880 generations in the monthly window, 1,222,092,604 in the 43-week window. A generation counts when a general-purpose generative model produced a new image from a prompt, with or without a reference image, in a generation flow: the AI image generator, the legacy text-to-image flows, the generative modes of the image editor, the image assistant, Mystic, and the illustrations generated inside Slidesgo presentations. Fixed-function tools are excluded even when they run on a generative model: retouch, reimagine, sketch, expand, restyle, upscalers, background removal, skin enhancer, outpainting, camera change, layer separation, icons, 3D and world generation, together 8.0% of the rows that output an image. Moderation passes and upscaling steps that run inside a generation flow are removed from the count (0.5%); they output no new image.

Definitions

A generation counts as successful when it returns status 200. A model here is a public model: the same model served through several integration routes is counted once, and where a version number covers two products (Flux 2 Pro and Flux 2 Klein, Flux Kontext and Flux 1 Dev) the flow name tells them apart. This departs from the strict provider-model-version key used in the video notes, because in image the same model arrives through up to four routes; the ranking of the top models is the same with either key. Mystic, Freepik’s own flow built on third-party models, counts as its own model. Google’s models are named as Google names them: Nano Banana (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image), Nano Banana Pro (Gemini 3 Pro Image), Nano Banana 2 (Gemini 3.1 Flash Image, including the Lite variant).

A model “launches” the first complete week it reaches 0.5% of weekly images after the first week of the window. Half-life is the number of weeks between a model’s peak share and the first week it holds less than half of that peak, whatever the reason. Image-to-image means the generation had an image among its inputs; text-to-image had none. The image-to-image split is computed without the 5.0% of generations served through one integration route that does not record inputs consistently, so Z-Image, almost entirely on that route, has no split. Makers are the companies that own the model; integration routers are not makers. Full definitions in the Report Glossary.

Limitations

1. Usage is not quality
Nothing here says which model makes the best image, and only models available on the platform are measured. Midjourney isn't on the platform. We don't compare prices or free tiers, so this report doesn't say which generator is the best free one.
2. August's leader won by a narrow margin
Seedream 5 beat Nano Banana 2 by 0.4 points in August, inside what a single month can resolve; in the weekly data Seedream 5 has been ahead since the week of August 10.
3. Two models were already big when the data starts
Nano Banana was already at its peak in the first week of our data, so its 5 weeks are counted from the edge of the window, not from its real peak; Seedream 4 and Nano Banana were both launched before the window, so they have no time-to-peak.
4. Half-life measures loss of share, whatever the cause
A model replaced by its own successor counts the same as a model people stopped choosing.
5. Most of the rise in edits is model mix
A shift-share decomposition attributes 19.9 of the 18.4 points to which models people use and -1.5 points to changes within models. Slidesgo's automatic illustrations, 2.7% of the population, are text-only and account for part of Flux 2 Klein's and Flux 1 Dev's text-to-image weight.
6. Six days with an empty model field
From January 30 to February 4, 2026, the model field was empty on Black Forest Labs generations (0.13% of the population); they were assigned to their Flux product by flow name.
7. The interface comparison starts in June
Only the period from June 9, 2026, when API, MCP and agent traffic can be attributed, is compared; before that date, surfaces are mixed.

Reproducibility

Every number was independently recomputed by a second pass with its own queries before publication: the population and its ten monthly totals, the monthly shares of 23 models, the concentration table, the image-to-image split by model and by month, the maker shares, the surface comparison, and the launch, peak and half-life of every model recomputed from the weekly series. Fourteen counter-queries, all reconciled within 0.06 points.

Cite & data

Cite this report

Citation

Magnific (2026). No AI image model stayed on top for six months. Creative Signals, September 2026. magnific.com/blog/ai-image-models

Short form for press

“The most used AI image model changed three times in ten months: across 1.2 billion images generated on Magnific and Freepik between November 2025 and August 2026, Seedream 4, Seedream 4.5, Nano Banana 2 and Seedream 5 each held the top spot, and the window leader, Nano Banana 2, made 21.0% of images. Three in four AI images started from another image.”

entry.title: How to Create an AI Short Film with Magnific: Out Loud
entry.summary: Learn how to create an AI short film with Magnific, from character design to cinematic sequences, using the Out Loud workflow and 22 prompts.
entry.content:
Learn how to create an AI short film with Magnific, from character design to cinematic sequences, using the Out Loud workflow and 22 prompts.

Creating an AI short film means making decisions that hold together across every scene: who the character is, how the world looks, what a performance communicates, and when to cut.

In Out Loud, we follow Luca from private bedroom rehearsals to a talent-show audition, where judgment begins before the first note. The story unfolds through small details: a hand tightening around a backpack, a nervous glance, a child repeating an adult’s reaction.

Here, we break down how the film was made with Magnific, from character design in Nano Banana Pro to video generation with Seedance 2.5 Draft. You’ll find 22 prompts covering character variations, locations, individual shots, and multishot sequences, along with practical guidance for adapting the workflow to your own film.

How to create an AI short film with Magnific

The workflow starts with a consistent set of visual references. Develop your character, establish the environments, and prepare recurring props before generating the scenes. Then direct the action shot by shot and bring the selected footage into your edit.

For Out Loud, the workflow combined:

  • Nano Banana Pro in Magnific for character and location images.
  • Magnific stock assets and Designer for the audition flyer.
  • Seedance 2.5 Draft in Magnific for video sequences, followed by conversion to HD.
  • Adobe After Effects for post-production.
  • Adobe Premiere Pro for editing.

Each stage serves a different creative decision. The images establish what belongs in the world. The video prompts direct what happens within it. The edit determines how those moments build into a story.

Before you use the prompts

The prompts below retain their original Spanish and English wording, with internal asset IDs replaced by readable reference names.

Attach your own reference images wherever a prompt calls for a character, location, or prop. A label such as @LUCA_CASA identifies a reference; typing the label alone will not supply the image.

Prepare these assets before generating:

  • Character references: one approved identity, plus the outfits needed for each scene.
  • Bedroom references: variations for daytime, nighttime, and different states of tidiness.
  • Audition references: the stage, judges, venue exterior, and waiting area.
  • Graphic props: a finished flyer, event sign, and calendar.

The collection includes alternate versions of some scenes. Use the version that fits your shot list, and adapt the durations to your sequence.

1. Create a consistent AI character with Nano Banana Pro

Start with the casting portrait. Luca’s design specifies hair, complexion, skin texture, expression, and lighting before introducing a setting or action. This gives the character a clear visual identity that can carry across the film.

Once you have an approved portrait, use it as a reference for the wardrobe variations. Check the face, haircut, and proportions each time. The audition outfit, pajamas, and everyday looks should all feel like the same person at different moments.

Neutral backgrounds keep the focus on those decisions. You can assess character continuity before adding the complexity of a bedroom, bus, or stage.

Prompt 1: Cast Luca

Director de casting cinematográfico, fondo de estudio neutro gris azulado, luz plana y fría con un ligero tono azul-verdoso (cool cinematic grade). Adolescente de 15 años, sin género definido, complexión gorda, piel pálida con textura realista (pecas y textura natural, sin retocar). Corte de pelo mullet ondulado y rubio por la parte interna de abajo, con flequillo recto y corto justo por encima de las cejas, pelo castaño oscuro con volumen natural, más corto arriba y en el flequillo, más largo y suelto por detrás y a los lados. Maquillaje sutil tipo delineado ligeramente corrido/ahumado, como si se lo hubiera hecho ella misma sin mucha técnica, labios naturales. Expresión seria mirando a cámara, fotografía de casting. Camiseta básica blanca.

Prompt 2: Create the audition outfit

viste a @img1con esta ropa **Prenda superior:** Chaqueta deportiva tipo track jacket, cuello alto con cremallera, color azul marino con panel de cuello y puños en rojo, franjas de rayas diagonales en tonos burdeos/rojo oscuro sobre los hombros y mangas (sin ningún logo, escudo ni texto — superficie lisa donde iría el emblema). Before export, review the film for character continuity, wardrobe, room layout, props, stage geography, and crop. Watch it once without sound to check whether the gestures and reactions communicate on their own.

3D figurines in 2026 span a longer chain than most people expect when they tap "generate." A collectible on your desk might start as concept art, become a triangle mesh, survive Blender cleanup, slice for resin or FDM, and end in a product photo for Shopify. AI shortcuts the middle steps, but it does not erase them.

The hard part is not the first cute render. It is wall thickness for printing, support strategy under chins and capes, scale when a 32 mm tabletop mini shares a build plate with a 6-inch display piece, and likeness when the figurine is supposed to be a specific person.

Magnific owns the upstream lane: character concept art, orthographic reference sheets, upscaled textures, packaging mockups, and team review before any mesher touches the file.

Concept art, printable meshes, and finished prints: three stages

Stage one is look development. You lock silhouette, costume, and paint scheme in 2D. Magnific image generation with reference images and Custom Characters keeps the same hero readable across front, side, and three-quarter views sculptors expect.

Stage two is mesh generation. Meshy, Tripo3D, and Kaedim lift concept renders into GLB or OBJ files. Single-image lifts guess hidden sides. Multi-view orthographic uploads produce stabler miniatures when you invest in Stage one.

Stage three is fabrication. Blender repairs non-manifold edges, adds print bases, and exports STL. Shapeways or your bench printer turns resin into object. Polycam enters when you scan a clay sculpt or an existing figurine to digitize instead of generating from scratch.

Best 8 tools for 3D figurines in every workflow in 2026

1. Magnific

Magnific is not a slicer and does not ship STL files from a single button. It is the art direction hub that makes downstream meshes less embarrassing.

The AI image generator produces hero figurine concepts, turnaround sheets, and accessory callouts with multi-model access (Flux, Imagen, Nano Banana, Seedream, and others). Upload reference photos when the figurine must match a person or mascot. Custom Characters help when the same character needs ten pose variants before sculpt approval.

Run finals through the image upscaler so texture detail survives the trip into Meshy or Tripo3D. The Mockup Generator documents Packaging templates and prompt-mode scenes for product shots when the figurine ships in a box, not loose in a bubble mailer. Spaces archives approved orthographic sets so factory partners and print vendors pull the same revision.

Character identity across a figurine line overlaps with our AI character generator workflows when the mini is part of a broader IP bible.

2. Meshy

Meshy is the default next step after Magnific concept art for indie creators who want a mesh tonight, not next sprint. Text and image inputs produce textured GLB files suited to stylized characters, pets, and chunky tabletop props.

Exports still need Blender passes for print bases, wall thickness, and support planning. Meshy shines on playful figurines where CAD precision matters less than readable silhouette at arm's length.

3. Tripo3D

Tripo3D focuses on fast single-image lifts with optional LOD-friendly outputs. Feed a clean Magnific front and side render pair when one view alone collapses a cape or ponytail.

Hero film characters will need manual retopo. Gift figurines and pitch maquettes often ship before that polish is worth the labor.

4. Polycam

Polycam digitizes physical figurines, clay maquettes, and garage kit prototypes through LiDAR and photogrammetry on phone or iPad. Use it when the master sculpt already exists and you need a mesh for scaling, duplication, or AR preview.

Glass-heavy display cases and mirror bases still fight any scanner. Matte spray and controlled light help.

5. Blender

Blender is the free cleanup room every figurine pipeline eventually touches. Import AI mesh, delete floating triangles, solidify thin cloaks, boolean union the figure to a pedestal, and export STL for resin.

No AI button replaces measuring wall thickness in millimeters before you waste resin on a hollow shell that cracks at the ankles.

6. Shapeways

Shapeways prints your STL in nylon, resin, or metal when you do not own a bench printer. Upload from Blender, pick material, and ship direct to customers for limited merch drops.

Unit economics matter. A six-inch figurine in premium resin is a gift price point, not a impulse-cart add-on, unless you batch many copies on one plate.

7. Kaedim

Kaedim targets teams that want human-assisted production meshes from concept art. You upload Magnific turnarounds, Kaedim returns cleaner topology than raw single-click generators, at higher cost and longer turnaround.

Studios launching a figurine SKU with retail packaging often pair Kaedim output with Magnific mockups for the same campaign asset folder.

8. Sloyd

Sloyd generates parametric 3D props and simple character bases you can kitbash under a hero sculpt. It is not a photo figurine service, but indie tabletop designers use it to flood terrain and weapon variants while the character mesh comes from Meshy or Tripo.

Expect stylized game readability, not hyper-real celebrity likeness.

How these 8 tools compare

Use Magnific for everything before the mesh exists: concept, orthographics, upscale, packaging mockups, and version control in Spaces. Meshy and Tripo3D lead fast AI mesh generation from that art. Polycam leads when the master is physical clay. Blender leads repair and STL export. Shapeways leads outsourced printing. Kaedim leads production-grade topology from art handoff. Sloyd leads parametric kitbash parts for game-scale minis.

If you only need a 2D collectible poster, stay in Magnific and skip mesh tools. If you need a desk figurine, budget Magnific plus Meshy or Tripo plus Blender minimum. If you need retail volume, add Kaedim review and factory QC beyond any single generator.

Magnific workflow: art direction before you mesh

Write a brief: scale (32 mm mini vs 6-inch display), material look (matte PVC vs glossy resin), and whether the figurine is a person, pet, or creature.

Generate front, side, and three-quarter views in the AI image generator with the same reference lock. Label accessories separately so weapons do not merge into torsos in the mesh pass.

Upscale approved sheets. Export PNG orthographics. Upload to Meshy or Tripo3D. Download GLB, import to Blender, merge to base, check wall thickness, export STL.

Render a product mock in the Mockup Generator with Packaging templates for pitch decks and preorder pages. Archive the full chain in Spaces for factory email threads.

Source photo figurines need cleaner plates first. Our AI photo generator guide covers lighting that survives later depth lifts when you start from a phone snap instead of illustration.

Print-ready figurine checklist

  • Wall thickness: aim for 1.5 to 2 mm on FDM prints; resin can go thinner with care and proper orientation.
  • Base or peg: add a flat pedestal or peg hole so the figure stands without tipping.
  • Internal cavities: delete hollow shells AI meshes often invent before slicing.
  • Support orientation: place supports where scars hide (under base, behind cape), not on the face.
  • Scale proof: print a small test slice before a full resin pour.
  • Accessory fit: dry-fit separate weapons and stands before gluing.
  • File versioning: name STL exports by revision so print vendors do not pull an outdated hollow file.

Gifts, tabletop minis, and merch drops

Custom wedding and anniversary gifts start from a couple photo, stylized in Magnific, meshed in Tripo, printed in white resin and hand-painted.

Tabletop RPG minis batch orthographic gens in Spaces, mesh in Meshy, base in Sloyd terrain, print armies on one plate.

Influencer merch pairs a limited figurine STL drop with Magnific mockup shots for the preorder page the same week.

Pet figurines need snout-forward reference photos with open eyes. Stylize fur in 2D before meshing so triangles do not become noise.

Factory licensing pitches ship Magnific blister mockups from the action figure article lane plus Kaedim mesh samples, not raw AI exports alone.

Common figurine print mistakes

  • Blurry source photos. A soft selfie will not produce a likeness-accurate mesh.
  • Missing side views. Single-angle lifts often hollow out cloaks and capes on the unseen side.
  • No solidify pass. Thin AI ankles and sword blades snap under normal handling.
  • Support scars on the hero angle. Orient the model so the face avoids support contact.
  • Wrong scale units. Mixing inches in the mesh with millimeters in the slicer shrinks or giants the print.
  • Marketing mismatch. Shipping STL revision four while mockups still show revision one confuses buyers.
  • Uncleared likeness. Celebrity figurines need publicity rights before commercial sale.

IP, likeness, and selling custom figurines

Usage rights vary by asset, tool, model, and plan. Check the current Magnific Terms of Use and any model-specific terms before client or resale work. Custom figurines of real people require consent. Fan figurines of franchise characters need license rights for sold products, not just personal shelf display.

AI meshes are not engineering sign-off. Safety testing for toys with small parts applies to gifts for children under regulatory thresholds in your market.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I make a 3D figurine from a photo?

Stylize the photo in Magnific, export clean orthographic views, upload to Meshy or Tripo3D, repair in Blender, then print at home or via Shapeways.

Can Magnific print a figurine directly?

No. Magnific generates and upscales 2D concept art and packaging mockups. You export meshes from dedicated 3D tools and slice for print separately.

What is the best AI tool for 3D figurines?

Magnific for concept and mockups, Meshy or Tripo3D for meshes, Blender for print prep. Pick based on whether you start from art, photos, or clay.

Resin or FDM for custom figurines?

Resin wins fine detail on faces and capes. FDM wins large chunky sculpts and fast iteration when layer lines are acceptable.

How big should a desk figurine be?

Common display sizes are 3 to 6 inches tall plus base. Tabletop minis are often 28 to 32 mm scale to the eye line.

Can I sell 3D printed figurines?

Yes when you own IP rights and follow Magnific and mesh tool terms. You still need likeness consent and trademark clearance for commercial characters.
